title: Alpha Diversity
text: Alpha diversity measures diversity within single sample. ecodive, metrics grouped four categories based aspect diversity quantify.

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Richness metrics estimate number distinct features (e.g., genera) sample. simplest metric, observed(), counts features non-zero abundance. Chao1 estimator extends inferring number unobserved, low-abundance features based ratio singletons (counts == 1) doubletons (counts == 2).
code: # Equivalent to rowSums(counts > 0) observed(counts) #> Saliva   Gums   Nose  Stool  #>      4      3      4      5 # Infers 8 unobserved genera chao1(c(1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 5, 5, 5)) #> [1] 16  # Infers less than 1 unobserved genera chao1(c(1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 5, 5, 5)) #> [1] 8.125  # Datasets without 1s and 2s give Inf or NaN chao1(counts) #> Saliva   Gums   Nose  Stool  #>    4.5    3.0    NaN    Inf

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Diversity metrics account richness evenness (equally abundances distributed). Simpson’s index often used measure evenness, representing probability two randomly selected individuals belong different species. Shannon diversity index (entropy) another common metric weights richness evenness.
code: # High Evenness (0.8) vs Low Evenness (0.07) simpson(c(20, 20, 20, 20, 20)) #> [1] 0.8 simpson(c(100, 1, 1, 1, 1)) #> [1] 0.07507396  # Stool < Gums < Saliva < Nose sort(simpson(counts)) #>      Stool       Gums     Saliva       Nose  #> 0.02302037 0.18806133 0.50725478 0.63539593 # High richness, High evenness shannon(rep(100, 100)) #> [1] 4.60517  # Stool < Gums < Saliva < Nose sort(shannon(counts)) #>      Stool       Gums     Saliva       Nose  #> 0.07927797 0.35692121 0.74119910 1.10615349

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Dominance metrics focus abundance common species. Berger-Parker index proportional abundance single abundant feature.

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Given: n : Number features (e.g. species, OTUs, ASVs). X_i : Integer count -th feature. X_T : Total counts (sequencing depth). X_T = \sum_{=1}^{n} X_i P_i : Proportional abundance -th feature. P_i = X_i / X_T F_1 : Number singletons (X_i = 1). F_2 : Number doubletons (X_i = 2).

title: Alpha Diversity
text: Given: r : Rare cutoff (features \le r counts considered rare). F_{rare} : Number rare features. F_{abund} : Number abundant features (> r counts). X_{rare} : Total counts belonging rare features. C_{ace} : Sample abundance coverage estimator. \gamma_{ace}^2 : Estimated coefficient variation. C_{ace} = 1 - \frac{F_1}{X_{rare}} \gamma_{ace}^2 = \max\left[\frac{F_{rare} \sum_{=1}^{r}(-1)F_i}{C_{ace}X_{rare}(X_{rare} - 1)} - 1, 0\right] D_{ace} = F_{abund} + \frac{F_{rare}}{C_{ace}} + \frac{F_1}{C_{ace}}\gamma_{ace}^2

text: following prompt provided Google Gemini 3’s “Thinking” model package:
code: I am analyzing the [PACKAGE_NAME] R package to compare the number of ecologically relevant alpha and beta diversity metrics it provides. The package's reference manual is attached.   Please act as an expert in ecological bioinformatics. Carefully read the manual and adhere to these rules:  1. DEFINITION OF A SUITABLE METRIC:    - ECOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Only include metrics used to quantify community diversity. This includes measures of richness, evenness, dominance, turnover, or nestedness.    - SYMMETRY REQUIREMENT: Strictly ignore any asymmetric metrics (where $d(a, b) \neq d(b, a)$). All included beta diversity metrics must be symmetric.    - EXCLUSIONS: Do NOT count accessory functions, data manipulation, plotting functions, or general statistical correlations (e.g., Pearson/Spearman) unless they are explicitly implemented as a community diversity or dissimilarity index.  2. DISTINCTNESS RULE:    - ARGUMENTS AS METRICS: If a single function computes different named metrics based on a character argument (e.g., `method="bray"` vs `method="jaccard"`), each valid method counts as a SEPARATE metric.    - NAMED METRIC SELECTORS: If a numeric parameter (like q, alpha, or p) is used to dial in specific named indices (e.g., q=0 for Richness, q=1 for Shannon, q=2 for Simpson, or phylogenetic equivalents like Faith's PD, Allen's H, and Rao's Q), count each named case as a distinct metric. Do not count intermediate or arbitrary numeric values.    - THE BINARY TOGGLE: Treat the presence-absence version and abundance-based version of the same metric as ONE entity, unless they are provided as separate functions or separate named methods in a list.    - UNIFRAC EXCEPTION: Count unweighted, weighted, weighted normalized, generalized, and variance-adjusted UniFrac as separate metrics if explicitly supported.  3. CATEGORIZATION:    - ALPHA DIVERSITY: Metrics that quantify the diversity of a single sample or site (inventory diversity).    - BETA DIVERSITY: Metrics that quantify the difference or dissimilarity between a pair of samples (differentiation diversity).  To ensure accuracy, format your response as follows:  - **Candidate Extraction:** List all potential diversity functions and their associated methods/parameters found in the manual. - **Evaluation:** Filter the candidates against the "Symmetry," "Ecological Relevance," and "Distinctness" rules. - **Categorized Metric List:** Provide a table or list of all validated metrics with two columns: [Metric Name] and [Category (Alpha or Beta)]. - **Final Summary:**     - **Total Alpha Diversity Metrics:** [Integer]     - **Total Beta Diversity Metrics:** [Integer]     - **UniFrac Metrics Present:** [Yes/No]

code: ord <- pca(iris[, 1:4], scale = TRUE)  attr(ord, 'loadings') #>                     PC1        PC2        PC3 #> Sepal.Length  0.5210659 0.37741762 -0.7195664 #> Sepal.Width  -0.2693474 0.92329566  0.2443818 #> Petal.Length  0.5804131 0.02449161  0.1421264 #> Petal.Width   0.5648565 0.06694199  0.6342727  load <- attr(ord, 'loadings') * 3 plot(ord, col = iris$Species, asp = 1) arrows(0, 0, load[, 1], load[, 2], length = 0.1) text(load[, 1:2], labels = rownames(load), pos = 4) all.equal(abs(pca(iris[, 1:4])[, 1]), abs(pcoa(euclidean(iris[, 1:4]))[, 1])) #> [1] TRUE ord <- rpca(iris[, 1:4]) round(100 * attr(ord, 'prop'), 1) #> [1] 96.8  2.7  0.5

code: set.seed(1) taxa   <- colnames(ex_counts) grad   <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 30) counts <- sapply(seq_along(taxa), function (j) rpois(30, 3 * exp(grad * (j - 3.5)))) dimnames(counts) <- list(paste0('S', 1:30), taxa)  bc <- pcoa(bray(counts), n_axes = 2) uf <- pcoa(unweighted_unifrac(counts, tree = ex_tree), n_axes = 2)  fit <- procrustes(uf, bc, symmetric = TRUE) attr(fit, 'ss') #> [1] 0.4595868  procrustes_test(uf, bc) #> Procrustes randomization test (PROTEST) #>  #> r = 0.7351, p = 0.001, z =  6.67 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Symmetric Procrustes sum of squares (m^2): 0.4596 #> Samples: 30, axes: 2 xy <- attr(fit, 'target') plot(xy, asp = 1, pch = 16, xlab = 'Axis 1', ylab = 'Axis 2') arrows(xy[, 1], xy[, 2], fit[, 1], fit[, 2], length = 0.05, col = 'grey40')

what: The Optimal Input: Compressed Sparse Matrices
title: Performance Guide
text: ecodive highly efficient reformatting data internally one-calculations. need manually format data single function calls. However, plan run multiple ecodive functions large dataset, see performance benefit converting data optimal format first. format column-compressed sparse matrix (dgCMatrix) Matrix package, samples arranged columns. conversion , prevent ecodive reformat data subsequent function call.
code: library(ecodive) library(Matrix)  # Assume 'my_counts' is a standard matrix with samples in rows my_counts <- as.matrix(ex_counts)  # Convert once to the optimal format optimal_counts <- as(t(my_counts), "dgCMatrix")  # Now, run multiple analyses on the pre-formatted object. # Remember to specify margin = 2L since samples are in columns. shannon_vals <- shannon(optimal_counts, margin = 2L) simpson_vals <- simpson(optimal_counts, margin = 2L) observed_vals <- observed(optimal_counts, margin = 2L)

title: Performance Guide
text: Many diversity metrics operate transformed data, commonly relative abundances (norm = 'percent'). specify transformation like norm = 'percent', ecodive performs conversion internally. adds small amount computational overhead. plan run many different analyses transformed data, efficient perform transformation pass pre-transformed data ecodive, specifying norm = 'none'.
code: # Inefficient: Transforming the data twice shannon_vals <- shannon(optimal_counts, norm = 'percent', margin = 2L) simpson_vals <- simpson(optimal_counts, norm = 'percent', margin = 2L)  # More Efficient: Transform once rel_abund <- t(apply(t(optimal_counts), 1, function(x) x / sum(x))) rel_abund <- as(rel_abund, "dgCMatrix")  shannon_vals <- shannon(rel_abund, norm = 'none', margin = 2L) simpson_vals <- simpson(rel_abund, norm = 'none', margin = 2L)

title: Performance Guide
text: one exception rule centered log-ratio transformation (norm = 'clr'), used calculating Aitchison distance. standard CLR workflow requires replacing zeros small pseudocount transformation (since log(0) undefined). replacement step instantly turns sparse matrix (mostly zeros) fully dense matrix (zeros), dramatically increases memory consumption. ecodive’s implementation CLR-compatible beta diversity metrics pseudocount-aware. Instead modifying entire matrix memory, C engine applies pseudocount dynamically distance calculation. allows input matrix remain sparse enables algorithm work directly original data pointer without creating massive, dense copy matrix object. Therefore, CLR-based metrics, achieve significantly better performance lower memory usage letting ecodive handle transformation. : :
code: # Best for CLR: Let ecodive handle the transformation dynamically aitchison_dist <- aitchison(optimal_counts, margin = 2L, pseudocount = 0.5) # Inefficient for CLR: Adding pseudocounts creates a dense matrix library(compositions) dense_matrix   <- clr(t(as.matrix(optimal_counts)) + 0.5) # Becomes dense aitchison_dist <- euclidean(dense_matrix, norm = 'none')

title: UniFrac Calculations
text: Lozupone et al, 2005: Unweighted UniFrac R Package ecodive: unweighted_unifrac() R Package abdiv: unweighted_unifrac() R Package phyloseq: UniFrac(weighted=FALSE) R Package OmicFlow: unifrac(weighted=FALSE) qiime2 qiime diversity beta-phylogenetic --p-metric unweighted_unifrac mothur: unifrac.unweighted() First, transform B presence (1) absence (0) indicators. \begin{align*}  &= \{9, 0, 0, 0, 9, 6, 3, 3\} \\ ' &= \{1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1\} \end{align*} \begin{align*} B  &= \{7, 5, 1, 4, 2, 8, 8, 0\} \\ B' &= \{1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0\} \end{align*} apply formula: \begin{align*} U &= \displaystyle \frac{\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i(|'_i - B'_i|)}{\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i(max('_i,B'_i))}  \\ \\ U &= \displaystyle \frac{L_1(|'_1-B'_1|) + L_2(|'_2-B'_2|) + \cdots + L_n(|'_n-B'_n|)}{L_1(max('_1,B'_1)) + L_2(max('_2,B'_2)) + \cdots + L_n(max('_n,B'_n))}  \\ \\ U &= \displaystyle \frac{0.2(|1-1|) + 0.4(|0-1|) + \cdots + 0.3(|1-0|)}{0.2(max(1,1)) + 0.4(max(0,1)) + \cdots + 0.3(max(1,0))}  \\ \\ U &= \displaystyle \frac{0.2(0) + 0.4(1) + 0.8(1) + 0.5(1) + 0.9(0) + 0.6(0) + 0.7(0) + 0.3(1)}{0.2(1) + 0.4(1) + 0.8(1) + 0.5(1) + 0.9(1) + 0.6(1) + 0.7(1) + 0.3(1)}  \\ \\ U &= \displaystyle \frac{0.4 + 0.8 + 0.5 + 0.3}{0.2 + 0.4 + 0.8 + 0.5 + 0.9 + 0.6 + 0.7 + 0.3}  \\ \\ U &= \displaystyle \frac{2}{4.4}  \\ \\ U &= 0.4545455 \end{align*}

title: UniFrac Calculations
text: Lozupone et al, 2007: Raw Weighted UniFrac R Package ecodive: weighted_unifrac() R Package abdiv: weighted_unifrac() R Package phyloseq: UniFrac(weighted=TRUE, normalized=FALSE) R Package OmicFlow: unifrac(weighted=TRUE, normalized=FALSE) qiime2 qiime diversity beta-phylogenetic --p-metric weighted_unifrac \begin{align*} W &= \sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i|\frac{A_i}{A_T} - \frac{B_i}{B_T}|  \\ \\ W &= L_1|\frac{A_1}{A_T} - \frac{B_1}{B_T}| + L_2|\frac{A_2}{A_T} - \frac{B_2}{B_T}| + \cdots + L_n|\frac{A_n}{A_T} - \frac{B_n}{B_T}|  \\ \\ W &= 0.2|\frac{9}{15} - \frac{7}{15}| + 0.4|\frac{0}{15} - \frac{5}{15}| + \cdots + 0.3|\frac{3}{15} - \frac{0}{15}|  \\ \\ W &= 0.02\overline{6} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.05\overline{3} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.42 + 0.08 + 0.2\overline{3} + 0.06  \\ \\ W &= 1.14 \end{align*}

title: UniFrac Calculations
text: Lozupone et al, 2007: Normalized Weighted UniFrac R Package ecodive: normalized_unifrac() R Package abdiv: weighted_normalized_unifrac() R Package phyloseq: UniFrac(weighted=TRUE, normalized=TRUE) R Package OmicFlow: unifrac(weighted=TRUE, normalized=TRUE) qiime2 qiime diversity beta-phylogenetic --p-metric weighted_normalized_unifrac mothur: unifrac.weighted() \begin{align*}  N &= \displaystyle \frac   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i|\frac{A_i}{A_T} - \frac{B_i}{B_T}|}   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i(\frac{A_i}{A_T} + \frac{B_i}{B_T})}   \\ \\    N &= \displaystyle \frac   {L_1|\frac{A_1}{A_T} - \frac{B_1}{B_T}| + L_2|\frac{A_2}{A_T} - \frac{B_2}{B_T}| + \cdots + L_n|\frac{A_n}{A_T} - \frac{B_n}{B_T}|}   {L_1(\frac{A_1}{A_T} + \frac{B_1}{B_T}) + L_2(\frac{A_2}{A_T} + \frac{B_2}{B_T}) + \cdots + L_n(\frac{A_n}{A_T} + \frac{B_n}{B_T})}   \\ \\    N &= \displaystyle \frac   {0.2|\frac{9}{15} - \frac{7}{15}| + 0.4|\frac{0}{15} - \frac{5}{15}| + \cdots + 0.3|\frac{3}{15} - \frac{0}{15}|}   {0.2(\frac{9}{15} + \frac{7}{15}) + 0.4(\frac{0}{15} + \frac{5}{15}) + \cdots + 0.3(\frac{3}{15} + \frac{0}{15})}   \\ \\    N &= \displaystyle \frac   {0.02\overline{6} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.05\overline{3} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.42 + 0.08 + 0.2\overline{3} + 0.06}   {0.21\overline{3} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.05\overline{3} + 0.1\overline{3} + 0.66 + 0.56 + 0.51\overline{3} + 0.06}   \\ \\    N &= \displaystyle \frac{1.14}{2.326667}  \\ \\ N &= 0.4899713 \end{align*}

title: UniFrac Calculations
text: Chen et al. 2012: Generalized UniFrac R Package ecodive: generalized_unifrac(alpha = 0.5) R Package abdiv: generalized_unifrac(alpha = 0.5) R Package GUniFrac: GUniFrac(alpha = 0.5) qiime2 qiime diversity beta-phylogenetic --p-metric generalized_unifrac -0.5 \begin{align*}  G &= \displaystyle \frac   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i(\frac{A_i}{A_T} + \frac{B_i}{B_T})^{\alpha}     |\displaystyle \frac       {\frac{A_i}{A_T} - \frac{B_i}{B_T}}       {\frac{A_i}{A_T} + \frac{B_i}{B_T}} |}   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i(\frac{A_i}{A_T} + \frac{B_i}{B_T})^{\alpha}}  \\ \\  G &= \displaystyle \frac   {     L_1(\frac{A_1}{A_T} + \frac{B_1}{B_T})^{0.5}       |\displaystyle \frac         {\frac{A_1}{A_T} - \frac{B_1}{B_T}}         {\frac{A_1}{A_T} + \frac{B_1}{B_T}}| +     \cdots +     L_n(\frac{A_n}{A_T} + \frac{B_n}{B_T})^{0.5}       |\displaystyle \frac         {\frac{A_n}{A_T} - \frac{B_n}{B_T}}         {\frac{A_n}{A_T} + \frac{B_n}{B_T}}|   }{     L_1(\frac{A_1}{A_T} + \frac{B_1}{B_T})^{0.5} +     \cdots +     L_n(\frac{A_n}{A_T} + \frac{B_n}{B_T})^{0.5}   }     \\ \\  G &= \displaystyle \frac   {     0.2(\frac{9}{15} + \frac{7}{15})^{0.5}       |\displaystyle \frac         {\frac{9}{15} - \frac{7}{15}}         {\frac{9}{15} + \frac{7}{15}}| +     \cdots +     0.3(\frac{3}{15} + \frac{0}{15})^{0.5}       |\displaystyle \frac         {\frac{3}{15} - \frac{0}{15}}         {\frac{3}{15} + \frac{0}{15}}|   }{     0.2(\frac{9}{15} + \frac{7}{15})^{0.5} +     \cdots +     0.3(\frac{3}{15} + \frac{0}{15})^{0.5}   }     \\ \\    G &\approx \displaystyle \frac   {0.03 + 0.23 + 0.21 + 0.26 + 0.49 + 0.08 + 0.27 + 0.13}   {0.21 + 0.23 + 0.21 + 0.26 + 0.77 + 0.58 + 0.60 + 0.13}   \\ \\    G &= \displaystyle \frac{1.701419}{2.986235}  \\ \\ G &= 0.569754  \end{align*}

text: Chang et al, 2011: Variance Adjusted Weighted (VAW) UniFrac R Package ecodive: variance_adjusted_unifrac() R Package abdiv: variance_adjusted_unifrac() qiime2 qiime diversity beta-phylogenetic --p-metric weighted_normalized_unifrac --p-variance-adjusted \begin{align*}  V &= \displaystyle \frac   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i\displaystyle \frac     {|\frac{A_i}{A_T} - \frac{B_i}{B_T}|}     {\sqrt{(A_i + B_i)(A_T + B_T - A_i - B_i)}} }   {\sum_{= 1}^{n} L_i\displaystyle \frac     {\frac{A_i}{A_T} + \frac{B_i}{B_T}}     {\sqrt{(A_i + B_i)(A_T + B_T - A_i - B_i)}} }  \\ \\  V &= \displaystyle \frac   {     L_1\displaystyle \frac     {|\frac{A_1}{A_T} - \frac{B_1}{B_T}|}     {\sqrt{(A_1 + B_1)(A_T + B_T - A_1 - B_1)}} +     \cdots +     L_n\displaystyle \frac     {|\frac{A_n}{A_T} - \frac{B_n}{B_T}|}     {\sqrt{(A_n + B_n)(A_T + B_T - A_n - B_n)}}   }{     L_1\displaystyle \frac     {\frac{A_1}{A_T} + \frac{B_1}{B_T}}     {\sqrt{(A_1 + B_1)(A_T + B_T - A_1 - B_1)}} +     \cdots +     L_n\displaystyle \frac     {\frac{A_n}{A_T} + \frac{B_n}{B_T}}     {\sqrt{(A_n + B_n)(A_T + B_T - A_n - B_n)}}   }     \\ \\  V &= \displaystyle \frac   {     0.2\displaystyle \frac     {|\frac{9}{15} - \frac{7}{15}|}     {\sqrt{(9 + 7)(15 + 15 - 9 - 7)}} +     \cdots +     0.3\displaystyle \frac     {|\frac{3}{15} - \frac{0}{15}|}     {\sqrt{(3 + 0)(15 + 15 - 3 - 0)}}   }{     0.2\displaystyle \frac     {\frac{9}{15} + \frac{7}{15}}     {\sqrt{(9 + 7)(15 + 15 - 9 - 7)}} +     \cdots +     0.3\displaystyle \frac     {\frac{3}{15} + \frac{0}{15}}     {\sqrt{(3 + 0)(15 + 15 - 3 - 0)}}   }     \\ \\    V &\approx \displaystyle \frac   {0.002 + 0.012 + 0.010 + 0.013 + 0.029 + 0.005 + 0.016 + 0.007}   {0.014 + 0.012 + 0.010 + 0.013 + 0.046 + 0.037 + 0.036 + 0.007}   \\ \\    V &= \displaystyle \frac{4.09389}{4.174402}  \\ \\ V &= 0.9807128  \end{align*}

title: Parallel and Memory-Efficient Ecological Diversity Analysis
text: Analyzing ecological diversity often computational bottleneck, especially large datasets. ecodive addresses providing: High Performance: ecodive written C parallelized using pthreads, making dramatically faster R packages. Benchmarks show can 14,000x faster use 200,000x less memory. Zero Dependencies: package external R dependencies, making lightweight, stable, easy install. also makes ideal secure backend R packages. Comprehensive Metrics: implements 14 alpha 37 beta diversity metrics, including classic phylogenetic-aware methods like Faith’s PD complete UniFrac family. Ordination Statistics: Ten ordination methods (PCoA, NMDS, UMAP, t-SNE, db-RDA, robust Aitchison PCA, ), biplots, five permutation tests (PERMANOVA, PERMDISP, ANOSIM, MRPP, Mantel), whole analysis needs package. Trusted Results: Every method tested established package replaces, vegan, ape, scikit-bio, scikit-learn, uwot, gemelli. Results identical number threads, random methods take seed. Ease Use: API simple integrates seamlessly popular bioinformatics packages like phyloseq rbiom.

title: Abundance-based Coverage Estimator (ACE) — ace
text: ACE metric separates features "abundant" "rare" groups based cutoff (usually 10 counts). assumes presence abundant species certain, true number rare species must estimated. Equations: $$C_{ace} = 1 - \frac{F_1}{X_{rare}}$$ $$\gamma_{ace}^2 = \max\left[\frac{F_{rare} \sum_{=1}^{r}(-1)F_i}{C_{ace}X_{rare}(X_{rare} - 1)} - 1, 0\right]$$ $$D_{ace} = F_{abund} + \frac{F_{rare}}{C_{ace}} + \frac{F_1}{C_{ace}}\gamma_{ace}^2$$ : \(r\) : Rare cutoff (default 10). Features \(\le r\) counts considered rare. \(F_i\) : Number features exactly \(\) counts. \(F_1\) : Number features \(X_i = 1\) (singletons). \(F_{rare}\) : Number rare features \(X_i \le r\). \(F_{abund}\) : Number abundant features \(X_i > r\). \(X_{rare}\) : Total counts belonging rare features. \(C_{ace}\) : sample abundance coverage estimator. \(\gamma_{ace}^2\) : estimated coefficient variation. Parameter: cutoff integer threshold distinguishing rare abundant species. Standard practice use 10.

title: Aitchison distance — aitchison
text: Aitchison distance defined : $$\sqrt{\sum_{=1}^{n} [(\ln{X_i} - X_L) - (\ln{Y_i} - Y_L)]^2}$$ : \(X_i\), \(Y_i\) : Absolute counts \(\)-th feature. \(X_L\), \(Y_L\) : Mean log abundances. \(X_L = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{=1}^{n} \ln{X_i}\). \(n\) : number features. Base R Equivalent:
code: x <- log((x + pseudocount) / exp(mean(log(x + pseudocount)))) y <- log((y + pseudocount) / exp(mean(log(y + pseudocount)))) sqrt(sum((x-y)^2)) # Euclidean distance

title: Aitchison distance — aitchison
text: Zeros undefined Aitchison (CLR) transformation. pseudocount NULL (default) zeros detected, function uses half minimum non-zero value (min(x[x>0]) / 2) issues warning. suppress warning, provide explicit value (e.g., 1). matters: choice pseudocount neutral; acts weighting factor can significantly distort downstream results, especially sparse datasets. See Gloor et al. (2017) Kaul et al. (2017) open-access discussions mathematical implications, Costea et al. (2014) impact community clustering.

title: Analysis of Similarities (ANOSIM) — anosim
code: # 30 samples in three treatment groups. The 'high' group has more     # of the first five genera.     set.seed(1)     counts <- matrix(rpois(30 * 20, 5), 30, 20)     rownames(counts) <- paste0('S', 1:30)     meta <- data.frame(       row.names = rownames(counts),       treatment = rep(c('ctrl', 'low', 'high'), each = 10),       site      = rep(c('A', 'B'), 15) )     high <- meta$treatment == 'high'     counts[high, 1:5] <- counts[high, 1:5] + 5      dm <- bray(counts)      # Are samples more alike within treatment groups than between them?     anosim(dm, 'treatment', meta) #> Analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) #>  #> R = 0.3217, p = 0.001, z = 6.742 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Mean rank of the distances, between and within groups: #>         pairs mean_rank #> Between   300   239.712 #> ctrl       45   221.111 #> high       45    43.500 #> low        45   244.644      # The same, with the groups as a vector.     anosim(dm, meta$treatment) #> Analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) #>  #> R = 0.3217, p = 0.001, z = 6.742 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Mean rank of the distances, between and within groups: #>         pairs mean_rank #> Between   300   239.712 #> ctrl       45   221.111 #> high       45    43.500 #> low        45   244.644      # Permuting treatment labels only within each site.     anosim(dm, 'treatment', meta, strata = 'site') #> Analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) #>  #> R = 0.3217, p = 0.001, z = 6.714 #> Permutations: 999 (within strata) #>  #> Mean rank of the distances, between and within groups: #>         pairs mean_rank #> Between   300   239.712 #> ctrl       45   221.111 #> high       45    43.500 #> low        45   244.644      # Mean rank of the distances between and within groups.     anosim(dm, 'treatment', meta)$ranks #>         pairs mean_rank #> Between   300  239.7117 #> ctrl       45  221.1111 #> high       45   43.5000 #> low        45  244.6444      # Each pair of treatments, with Holm-adjusted p-values.     anosim(dm, 'treatment', meta, pairwise = TRUE)$pairwise #>                     R         z  n n_perm p_value p_adjusted #> ctrl-high  0.56455556  8.928828 20    999   0.001      0.003 #> ctrl-low  -0.08133333 -1.223469 20    999   0.889      0.889 #> high-low   0.45800000  7.884991 20    999   0.001      0.003

title: Correspondence Analysis (CA) — ca
text: Method \(P\) table divided grand total, \(r\) \(c\) row column sums (sample feature weights), correspondence analysis (Legendre & Legendre 2012, §9.2; Greenacre 2007) finds principal components matrix chi-square residuals \(\bar{Q} = D_r^{-1/2} (P - rc^T) D_c^{-1/2}\). \(\bar{Q} = U \Sigma V^T\), eigenvalues squared singular values, site scores (scaling 2) \(D_r^{-1/2} U\), species scores \(D_c^{-1/2} V \Sigma\). axes come block Lanczos iteration, needs products \(\bar{Q}\) vectors time. \(\bar{Q}\) sparse matrix less rank-one term, computed parallel table's non-zero values alone, sparse table never made dense. ca() shares solver cca(): ca(counts) gives scores, eigenvalues loadings cca(counts) constraints. CA PCA? title: Distance Test Wrapper Function — dist_test
code: # 30 samples in three treatment groups. The 'high' group has more     # of the first five genera.     set.seed(1)     counts <- matrix(rpois(30 * 20, 5), 30, 20)     rownames(counts) <- paste0('S', 1:30)     meta <- data.frame(       row.names = rownames(counts),       treatment = rep(c('ctrl', 'low', 'high'), each = 10),       ph        = round(rnorm(30, 7, 0.3), 1) )     high <- meta$treatment == 'high'     counts[high, 1:5] <- counts[high, 1:5] + 5      dm <- bray(counts)      dist_test(dm, 'permanova', 'treatment', meta) #> Permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) #>  #> F = 3.442, p = 0.001, z = 8.275 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Model R2 = 0.2032. Model tested as a whole: #>  #>          Df SumOfSqs     R2     F Pr(>F)     #> Model     2   0.1813 0.2032 3.442  0.001 *** #> Residual 27   0.7111 0.7968                  #> Total    29   0.8924 1.0000                  #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1      # Every test of treatment, as one table.     tests <- list_dist_tests(val = 'id', groups = 'categorical')     do.call(rbind, lapply(tests, function (m)       as.data.frame(dist_test(dm, m, 'treatment', meta, cpus = 1)) )) #>        test stat_name  statistic p_value         z n_perm #> 1    anosim         R  0.3216543   0.001  6.741598    999 #> 2      mrpp     delta  0.2243903   0.001 -7.321666    999 #> 3 permanova         F  3.4422193   0.001  8.274905    999 #> 4  permdisp         F 15.6818804   0.001 13.423920    999      # A numeric variable.     dist_test(dm, 'adonis2', 'ph', meta) #> Permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) #>  #> F = 0.3849, p = 0.972, z = -1.488 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Model R2 = 0.01356. Model tested as a whole: #>  #>          Df SumOfSqs     R2     F Pr(>F) #> Model     1   0.0121 0.0136 0.385  0.972 #> Residual 28   0.8803 0.9864              #> Total    29   0.8924 1.0000                  dist_test(dm, 'mantel', 'ph', meta, method = 'spearman') #> Mantel test (Spearman) #>  #> r = -0.0818, p = 0.863, z = -1.089 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Spearman's rank correlation rho #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30

code: # 30 samples along a pH gradient, which shifts the first five genera.     set.seed(1)     counts <- matrix(rpois(30 * 20, 5), 30, 20)     rownames(counts) <- paste0('S', 1:30)     ph <- setNames(round(runif(30, 6, 8), 1), rownames(counts))     counts[, 1:5] <- counts[, 1:5] + round(4 * (ph - 6))      dm <- bray(counts)      # Are samples that differ more in pH also more different in     # community composition?     mantel(dm, ph) #> Mantel test (Pearson) #>  #> r = 0.593, p = 0.001, z = 9.786 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Pearson's product-moment correlation #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30      # With rank correlation.     mantel(dm, ph, method = 'spearman') #> Mantel test (Spearman) #>  #> r = 0.5528, p = 0.001, z =    10 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Spearman's rank correlation rho #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30      # The same as a column of sample metadata.     meta <- data.frame(row.names = rownames(counts), ph = ph)     mantel(dm, 'ph', data = meta, method = 'spearman') #> Mantel test (Spearman) #>  #> r = 0.5528, p = 0.001, z =    10 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Spearman's rank correlation rho #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30      # Two distance matrices.     mantel(dm, dist(counts[, 6:20])) #> Mantel test (Pearson) #>  #> r = 0.4893, p = 0.001, z = 6.502 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Pearson's product-moment correlation #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30

code: # 30 samples along a pH gradient, which shifts the first five genera,     # at random locations.     set.seed(1)     counts <- matrix(rpois(30 * 20, 5), 30, 20)     rownames(counts) <- paste0('S', 1:30)     meta <- data.frame(       row.names = rownames(counts),       ph  = round(runif(30, 6, 8), 1),       lat = runif(30, 30, 35),       lon = runif(30, -100, -95) )     counts[, 1:5] <- counts[, 1:5] + round(4 * (meta$ph - 6))      dm  <- bray(counts)     geo <- dist(meta[, c('lat', 'lon')])      # Are samples that differ more in pH also more different in     # community composition, beyond the effect of geographic distance?     mantel_partial(dm, 'ph', given = geo, data = meta) #> Partial Mantel test (Pearson) #>  #> r = 0.5931, p = 0.001, z = 9.759 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Pearson's product-moment correlation #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30      # With rank correlation.     mantel_partial(dm, 'ph', given = geo, data = meta, method = 'spearman') #> Partial Mantel test (Spearman) #>  #> r = 0.5528, p = 0.001, z = 9.969 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Spearman's rank correlation rho #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30      # The same, through dist_test().     dist_test(dm, 'mantel_partial', 'ph', meta, given = geo, method = 'spearman') #> Partial Mantel test (Spearman) #>  #> r = 0.5528, p = 0.001, z = 9.969 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Correlation: Spearman's rank correlation rho #> Alternative: greater (r is more positive than by chance) #> Samples: 30

Parameter: power power parameter (default 1.5) determines value \(p\) equation. Special Cases Manhattan distance: \(p = 1\), formula reduces sum absolute differences. title: Morisita dissimilarity — morisita
text: Morisita dissimilarity defined : $$1 - \frac{2\sum_{=1}^{n}X_{}Y_{}}{\left(\frac{\sum_{=1}^{n}X_i(X_i - 1)}{X_T(X_T - 1)} + \frac{\sum_{=1}^{n}Y_i(Y_i - 1)}{Y_T(Y_T - 1)}\right)X_{T}Y_{T}}$$ : \(X_i\), \(Y_i\) : Absolute counts \(\)-th feature. \(X_T\), \(Y_T\) : Total counts sample. \(X_T = \sum_{=1}^{n} X_i\). \(n\) : number features. Base R Equivalent:
code: x <- ex_counts[1,] y <- ex_counts[2,] simpson_x <- sum(x * (x - 1)) / (sum(x) * (sum(x) - 1)) simpson_y <- sum(y * (y - 1)) / (sum(y) * (sum(y) - 1)) 1 - ((2 * sum(x * y)) / ((simpson_x + simpson_y) * sum(x) * sum(y)))

code: # 30 samples in three groups. The 'high' group is more variable.     set.seed(1)     counts <- matrix(rpois(30 * 20, 5), 30, 20)     rownames(counts) <- paste0('S', 1:30)     meta <- data.frame(       row.names = rownames(counts),       treatment = rep(c('ctrl', 'low', 'high'), each = 10) )     high <- meta$treatment == 'high'     counts[high, ] <- counts[high, ] * rpois(10 * 20, 1)      dm <- bray(counts)      # Do the treatment groups differ in dispersion?     res <- permdisp(dm, 'treatment', meta)     res #> Homogeneity of multivariate dispersions (PERMDISP) #>  #> F =  94.2, p = 0.001, z =  88.9 #> Permutations: 999 (free) #>  #> Distances to group centroids: #>   ctrl   high    low  #> 0.1640 0.3929 0.1698  #>  #>           Df Sum Sq Mean Sq    F N.Perm Pr(>F)     #> Groups     2 0.3406 0.17030 94.2    999  0.001 *** #> Residuals 27 0.0488 0.00181                        #> --- #> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1      # Each group's mean distance to its centroid.     res$dispersions #>      ctrl      high       low  #> 0.1640327 0.3928983 0.1698156       # Distances to spatial medians, as vegan::betadisper()'s default,     # with each pair of groups tested.     res <- permdisp(dm, meta$treatment, type = 'median', pairwise = TRUE)     res$pairwise #>                    t Df          z  n n_perm      p_value p_value_perm #> ctrl-high -9.0539173 18 -8.6372143 20    999 4.029174e-08        0.001 #> ctrl-low  -0.4405987 18 -0.3886739 20    999 6.647493e-01        0.662 #> high-low   8.6234560 18  8.4716805 20    999 8.282327e-08        0.001 #>             p_adjusted p_adjusted_perm #> ctrl-high 1.208752e-07           0.003 #> ctrl-low  6.647493e-01           0.662 #> high-low  1.656465e-07           0.003

text: Parsing follows Newick standard described https://evolution.genetics.washington.edu/phylip/newick_doc.html. Quoted labels. tip, internal node, root label may enclosed single quotes. Everything inside quotes taken literally, including parentheses, square brackets, colons, semicolons, commas, underscores, blanks, newlines. one exception two adjacent single quotes stand one literal apostrophe: '''s' read , '' empty label. Comments. Outside quotes, text square brackets (example [&rate=0.5]) comment ignored. Inside quotes, square brackets ordinary characters. Whitespace. Outside quotes, blanks around labels branch lengths ignored. line break, together blanks touching , removed entirely, label branch length wrapped across two lines rejoined. first tree (first ;) read. branch length root accepted discarded. Malformed input, unclosed quote, comment, parenthesis, raises error giving position problem.

title: Robust Aitchison distance — robust_aitchison
text: Robust Aitchison distance defined : $$\sqrt{\sum_{=1}^{n} (X^*_i - Y^*_i)^2}$$ : \(X^*_i\), \(Y^*_i\) : rclr-transformed counts \(\)-th feature. given sample \(X\), \(X^*_i = \ln(X_i) - X_L\) \(X_i > 0\), \(0\) otherwise. \(X_L\), \(Y_L\) : Mean log strictly positive abundances. \(X_L = \frac{1}{|P_X|}\sum_{j \P_X} \ln{X_j}\), \(P_X\) set indices \(X > 0\). \(|P_X|\), \(|P_Y|\) : number strictly positive features respective samples. \(n\) : total number features. Base R Equivalent:
code: x <- ifelse(x > 0, log(x) - mean(log(x[x > 0])), 0) y <- ifelse(y > 0, log(y) - mean(log(y[y > 0])), 0) sqrt(sum((x-y)^2)) # Euclidean distance

title: ecodive 2.3.2
text: Fixed aitchison(), every beta metric called norm = 'clr', returning NaN (, chebyshev(), wrong values) every sample pair. Two bugs involved: Data zeros (pseudocount 0) hit log(0) * 0, NaN. pseudocount truncated integer C, values 1, including automatic min(counts[counts > 0]) / 2, became 0, values like 1.5 silently rounded . gower() norm = 'clr' now computes feature’s range, distance features absent samples, feature’s CLR values instead treating absent features 0. gower() negative inputs (e.g. norm = 'rclr') now also uses full min--max range.

title: ecodive 2.3.1
text: CRAN release: 2026-11-05 read_tree() now handles quoted labels per Newick standard: '' inside quoted label decoded one literal apostrophe, '''s' read . Square brackets inside quotes literal characters rather comments, labels like 'o__[Saprospirales]' longer truncated. Newlines whitespace inside quotes preserved. Comments ([...]) outside quotes may contain apostrophes. read_tree() raises informative error, position problem, malformed input unclosed quote, comment, parenthesis. Previously return garbled tree. read_tree()’s parser now linear-time non-recursive, making 4x faster typical 100,000-tip tree much faster deep trees.
